analysis.one_liner: Lets union contracts require workers to join or pay the union, overriding state right-to-work laws.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on September 9, 2022 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the part of federal labor law that lets states pass 'right-to-work' rules. Today, those rules let workers in about half the states refuse to join the union at their workplace even if most of their coworkers voted to have one. Under this bill, a union contract could require every covered worker to join the union or pay it a fee as a condition of keeping the job, no matter what state law says.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in right-to-work states who want unions, and unions themselves. Unions would gain members and dues money in states where union contracts currently cannot require membership, and research on union security agreements links them to higher union coverage and stronger bargaining positions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Union workers and unions in right-to-work states

how_it_helps.text: Repeals section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act, the provision that lets states prohibit union security agreements, so federal law would no longer allow state right-to-work rules to block them.
Would authorize labor agreements to require membership in a labor organization as a condition of employment regardless of state law, preempting state prohibitions.

analysis.who_pays: Employers in right-to-work states, who would face stronger unions and likely higher wage and benefit costs, and workers who do not want to belong to a union, who would have to join or pay union fees to keep their jobs in unionized workplaces.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires workers who do not want union membership to join or pay the union anyway as a condition of employment, removing a choice that right-to-work laws currently give them in unionized workplaces.
Employers in right-to-work states would face strengthened unions, which they argue raises labor costs; the bill gives no opt-out for those states.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who want unions, this removes the biggest legal obstacle to union security in right-to-work states and would likely strengthen unions' bargaining power and finances there. The cost falls on workers who prefer not to join, who would lose the ability to stay nonmembers in a unionized shop, and on employers who would face more organized workforces. It is a straightforward trade of individual choice and employer leverage for collective worker power.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Labor Committee the same day, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Brad Sherman introduced the Nationwide Right to Unionize Act in the House on September 9, 2022.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on September 9, 2022.
Twenty-six members, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and workers who prefer not to join unions in right-to-work states are better off, since nothing changed. Unions and union-backed workers in those states gained nothing from an outcome that produced no vote at all.

for.name: Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Nationwide Right to Unionize Act on September 9, 2022.

against.name: Bobby Scott
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral and never scheduled it for a hearing, markup, or vote; the action history shows no activity after the referral.

against.name: House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Offered no cosponsorships; none of the bill's 27 supporters were Republicans, and right-to-work laws are a state-law priority conservatives defend.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's sponsor and 26 cosponsors was a Democrat, and no Republican signed on; even the Democratic-controlled committee did not take it up.

industries.note: The bill would let union contracts require membership or fees nationwide, expanding union membership and dues income, especially in right-to-work states. Unions argue that this strengthens collective bargaining, which raises pay and benefits for covered workers.
Stronger unions mean more organized workforces and likely higher wage and benefit costs for employers. Employers have historically backed right-to-work laws as a way to limit union power.
